content.text: Lenses are among the most important and widely used optical devices in the world. From the lenses in your eyes that allow you to read this text, to the lenses in cameras, microscopes, telescopes, and projectors, lenses shape how we see and interact with the world. A lens works by refracting light as it passes through a curved piece of transparent material, usually glass or plastic. By carefully choosing the shape and curvature of the lens surfaces, we can control how light is bent and where images are formed.

In this lesson, we will study the two main types of thin lenses, learn how to construct ray diagrams to determine the properties of images, and explore the mathematical relationships that govern lens behaviour. Understanding lenses is essential not only for physics but also for appreciating the technology that surrounds us in everyday life.

A lens is a piece of transparent material (usually glass or plastic) with at least one curved surface that refracts light to form an image. A thin lens is one whose thickness is small compared to its focal length and the distances involved. This simplification allows us to treat all the refraction as occurring at a single plane (the centre of the lens), making ray diagrams and calculations much simpler.

A converging lens, also called a convex lens, is thicker in the middle than at the edges. When parallel rays of light pass through a converging lens, they are refracted inwards and brought together (converge) at a single point called the principal focus or focal point.

Converging lenses can form both real and virtual images, depending on the position of the object relative to the focal point. They are used in magnifying glasses, cameras, projectors, and the human eye.

The shape of a converging lens causes light passing through the thicker central part to be refracted less than light passing through the thinner edges. The net effect is that parallel rays are brought to a focus.

A diverging lens, also called a concave lens, is thinner in the middle than at the edges. When parallel rays of light pass through a diverging lens, they are refracted outwards and spread apart (diverge). The diverging rays appear to come from a single point on the same side as the incoming light. This point is the principal focus of the diverging lens, and it is a virtual focal point because the light does not actually pass through it.

Diverging lenses always form virtual, upright, and diminished (smaller) images regardless of where the object is placed. They are used in spectacles for correcting short-sightedness (myopia) and in combination with converging lenses in complex optical instruments.
The straight line passing through the centre of the lens perpendicular to its surfaces. Rays along the principal axis pass straight through without being deflected.
The geometric centre of the lens. Rays passing through the optical centre are not deviated (they continue in a straight line).

The point at which rays parallel to the principal axis converge (for a converging lens) or appear to diverge from (for a diverging lens) after passing through the lens. Every lens has two focal points, one on each side, equidistant from the optical centre.
The distance from the optical centre of the lens to the principal focus. A shorter focal length means a more powerful lens that bends light more strongly.
The plane perpendicular to the principal axis at the focal point. Parallel rays that are not parallel to the principal axis converge at a point on the focal plane.
The point on the principal axis at a distance of twice the focal length from the optical centre. This point has special significance in image formation.

are formed when light rays actually converge and pass through the image point. Real images can be projected onto a screen. They are always formed on the opposite side of the lens from the object (for a single converging lens). Real images are inverted (upside down) relative to the object.

are formed when light rays appear to diverge from the image point, but do not actually pass through it. Virtual images cannot be projected onto a screen. They can only be seen by looking through the lens. Virtual images are upright (the same way up as the object).
To construct a ray diagram, we use three standard rays from the top of the object. Any two of these three rays are sufficient to locate the image:
A ray travelling parallel to the principal axis is refracted through the principal focus (F) on the other side of the lens.
A ray passing through the optical centre of the lens continues in a straight line without being deviated.
A ray passing through the principal focus (F) on the object's side of the lens is refracted parallel to the principal axis on the other side.
The point where any two of these rays intersect (or appear to intersect) after passing through the lens gives the position of the top of the image.

The three standard construction rays for a converging lens are:
A ray parallel to the principal axis refracts through F on the far side.
A ray through the optical centre passes straight through undeviated.
A ray through F on the near side refracts parallel to the principal axis.
Image Formation by a Converging Lens: Different Object Positions
Image is between F and 2F on the other side.
Image is real, inverted, and diminished (smaller than the object).
Application: the camera lens, where a large scene is captured as a small image on the film or sensor.
Image is at 2F on the other side.
Image is real, inverted, and the same size as the object.
Image is beyond 2F on the other side.
Image is real, inverted, and magnified (larger than the object).
Application: projectors, where a small slide or image is projected as a large image on a screen.
Object at F (at the focal point):
The refracted rays emerge parallel and never converge.
The image is formed at infinity.
No practical image is formed; the rays neither converge nor diverge.
Application: searchlights and collimators, where a parallel beam of light is needed.
Object inside F (between F and the lens):
The refracted rays diverge after passing through the lens.
The image is on the same side as the object.
Image is virtual, upright, and magnified.
Image Formation by a Diverging Lens
For a diverging lens, regardless of where the object is placed, the image is always:
Virtual (on the same side as the object)
Closer to the lens than the object
The ray diagram for a diverging lens uses similar rules:
A ray parallel to the principal axis diverges as though it came from the focal point on the same side as the incoming light.
A ray through the optical centre passes straight through.
A ray directed towards the focal point on the far side emerges parallel to the principal axis.

For a real image, the magnification is positive in magnitude but the image is inverted. For a virtual image formed by a converging lens (object inside F), the magnification is greater than 1 and the image is upright.
The power of a lens is a measure of how strongly it converges or diverges light. It is defined as the reciprocal of the focal length in metres:
Power is measured in dioptres (D). A lens with a focal length of 0.5 m has a power of

The following worked examples use the thin lens equation, magnification formula, and power of a lens, which go beyond the IGCSE syllabus. They are included for enrichment and are not required for your exam.
Example 1: Image Formation by a Converging Lens
An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the image distance and the magnification. Describe the image.
The image is 15 cm from the lens on the opposite side from the object. It is real, inverted, and diminished (half the size of the object). The object is beyond 2F (since
cm and the object is at 30 cm), and the image is between F and 2F (between 10 and 20 cm), which is consistent with our ray diagram rules.
An object is placed 6 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the image distance and magnification. Describe the image.
The negative sign indicates the image is virtual (on the same side as the object).

The image is virtual, upright, and magnified (2.5 times the size of the object). This is the principle behind a magnifying glass: placing the object inside the focal length produces an enlarged virtual image.
An object placed 20 cm from a converging lens produces a real image 20 cm on the other side. What is the focal length of the lens?
The focal length is 10 cm. Notice that the object and image are both at 2F (since
cm), and the image is the same size as the object, confirming the rule for objects at 2F.
An object that is 5 cm tall is placed 25 cm from a converging lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the image distance, magnification, and image height.
The image is real, inverted, magnified (1.5 times), and 7.5 cm tall.
A converging lens has a focal length of 25 cm. Calculate its power in dioptres.
The power of the lens is +4 D (positive because it is a converging lens).
Misconception 1: A larger lens produces a larger image

The size of the image depends on the focal length and the object distance, not the physical size of the lens. A larger lens collects more light and produces a brighter image, but not a larger one. The focal length and object position determine image size.
Misconception 2: Blocking half the lens removes half the image

If you cover half of a converging lens, you do not lose half the image. The full image is still formed, but it is dimmer because less light reaches the image. Every point on the lens contributes to every point of the image.
Misconception 3: Virtual images are not real

While it is true that virtual images cannot be projected onto a screen, they are certainly real in the sense that you can see them. When you use a magnifying glass, the magnified image you see is a virtual image, but it is perfectly visible to your eye. The word "virtual" in physics means that the light rays do not actually pass through the image location.
Misconception 4: Focal length depends on object distance

The focal length of a lens is a fixed property of the lens determined by its shape and material. It does not change when you move the object closer or farther from the lens. What changes is the image distance and the image properties.
Misconception 5: Diverging lenses cannot form useful images

Although diverging lenses only form virtual, diminished images on their own, they are extremely useful in combination with converging lenses. They are essential in correcting short-sightedness, in zoom lens systems, and in reducing aberrations in optical instruments.

A converging (convex) lens is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays to a focal point. A diverging (concave) lens is thinner in the middle and spreads parallel rays apart.
The focal length is the distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.
Three standard rays are used for ray diagrams: the parallel ray, the central ray, and the focal ray.

A converging lens produces different types of images depending on the object position: real and diminished (object beyond 2F), real and same size (object at 2F), real and magnified (object between F and 2F), image at infinity (object at F), or virtual and magnified (object inside F).
A diverging lens always produces a virtual, upright, diminished image.

The image is real, inverted, and magnified (twice the object size). The object is between F and 2F (since
cm, and the object is at 12 cm), so this is consistent with the expected image beyond 2F.

When the object is inside the focal length (closer to the lens than F), the light rays diverge after passing through the lens. They do not converge to form a real image. Instead, the diverging rays appear to come from a point on the same side as the object, producing a virtual, upright, and magnified image. The eye intercepts these diverging rays and the brain perceives a larger image.

If the object is moved beyond the focal length, the lens produces a real, inverted image on the far side of the lens. This image is inverted (upside down) and cannot serve as a useful magnified view. When the object is between F and 2F, the real image is magnified but inverted, so the magnifying glass no longer works as a simple magnifier for reading.
